title: Traffic continuity and progressive enablement notes
content:
Purpose:
This is a working note for cross-functional teams (product, infra, SRE, solutions) on an approach we can iterate on for progressive enablement, canaries, and A/B experimentation that focuses on traffic continuity — keeping customer-facing paths healthy while validating behavioral and performance hypotheses.

Context and motivation:
- We often conflate feature flag rollouts, canaries, and A/B experiments. This doc frames them as overlapping but distinct operations that share primitives (traffic slicing, metric guards, telemetry hooks).
- Recent incidents where a canary overloaded a downstream cache highlighted the need for a clear continuity-first playbook: routing logic, fast safety valves, and responsibilities.
- Goal: reduce cognitive overhead during launches; make rollouts faster and safer for teams new to Redwood’s advanced routing features.

Key concepts (working definitions):
- Progression vs Promotion: progression = gradual increase of exposure over time using pre-defined schedule or signals; promotion = handing control to a broader target (e.g., all paid customers).
- Signal-based promotion: advance when guards pass (latency, error budget, correctness checks).
- Time-based progression: deterministic timeline (useful when signals noisy).
- Continuity-first routing: always keep a path for healthy traffic to bypass the new variant automatically if primary signals degrade.

Minimum rollout primitives we expect teams to use:
- Traffic slice definitions: percentage, attributes (region, plan, device), sticky IDs for sessions/users.
- Observability hooks: synthesized metrics (slo_error_rate, p95_inference_latency, token-cost-per-response), and application-level correctness (sampled evals).
- Safety valves: immediate route switch, rate cap on new variant, global kill switch (feature flag), and fallback model variant mapping.
- Rollout metadata: owner, escalation contacts, Jira link, expected impact, rollback window.

Triage ownership matrix (quick reference):
- Product owner: business criteria, correctness hypotheses, communication to stakeholders.
- Release engineer / Platform: config of routing policy, rollout definition in console, bake-in of traffic caps.
- SRE/Infra: monitor infra signals (queue depth, gpu-util, pod restarts), execute emergency routing changes.
- Applied ML: verify model output quality for sampled sessions, analyze hallucination/metric drift.
- Customer success / Solutions: hold channel for affected customers, coordinate postmortem comms.

Suggested rollout template (fields to fill before enabling):
- Title / short description
- Owner and backup on-call
- Jira/PR references
- Release window and timezone
- Target segment (exact rule) and initial slice (e.g., 2% north-america-paid-users)
- Progression plan (2% -> 10% -> 50% -> 100%) and decision criteria for each step
- Technical guardrails (p95 latency < 400ms, error_rate < 0.5%, sampling QA pass rate > 95%)
- Observability dashboard and runbook link
- Rollback criteria and execution steps
- Post-rollout evaluation window and metrics owners

Concrete example (progressive enablement):
- Feature: response-shortening-with-kv-cache
- Initial slice: 1% of sessions (sticky by user id), NA region, non-enterprise tier
- Progression plan: 1% for 1h, if all guards pass -> 5% for 2h, then 25% for 4h, then 100% in 24h
- Guards per step:
  * infra: GPU queue depth < 70% of limit, no >=3 pod restarts in 15m window
  * perf: p95 latency change vs baseline < 1.25x and absolute p95 < 500ms
  * correctness: sampled responses (1/1000) must pass automated eval set >= 96%
  * cost: token-cost-per-response delta < $0.01
- Safety valves: immediate 100% traffic divert to previous model (console -> fast-fallback), feature-flag kill, automated alerting to on-call SRE.

A/B experimentation notes (keep it separate from rollout playbook):
- A/B experiments are hypothesis-driven: tie to single measurable KPI and statistical plan up-front.
- Randomization should be seeded at user or session level depending on metric scope. Avoid mixing sticky logic between A/B and feature flags.
- Use stratified splits when you expect heterogeneity (e.g., region or plan).
- Minimum detectable effect (MDE) guidance: compute sample sizes before start; if we can’t hit the sample size in the launch window, convert to a progressive rollout instead.
- Infrastructure constraints: A/B variants may have different resource profiles. Always include infra metrics in experiment dashboard.

Traffic continuity patterns and route primitives:
- Canary in-path (shared resources): run variant on same service cluster; cheaper but riskier for resource contention. Add stricter infra guards and rate caps.
- Canary shadowing (duplicate requests): safest for correctness validation but doubles downstream cost; useful when correctness > perf risk.
- Split-by-attribute vs weighted-percentage: prefer attribute when targeting cohorts (customers, regions) — gives more deterministic traffic and simpler rollback.
- Circuit-breaker routes: automatically redirect new-slice traffic to baseline once error thresholds reached.

Operational runbook (quick ops steps):
- Pre-flight (30–60m before): confirm dashboards live, escalation contacts reachable, infra quotas checked, create rollback plan ticket.
- Start: enable initial slice, tag release in event log (console), brief Slack channel.
- Monitor: first 15 minutes are high-sensitivity. Watch p50/p95/p99, error rate, downstream queues, sampling correctness.
- If guard breached: immediately throttle new-slice to 0% and notify SRE + Product. If noisy signals, roll back to previous mapping.
- Postmortem: capture timeline, metric deltas, root cause, mitigation, follow-up action (owner).

Open questions / tradeoffs we should decide: (TODO list)
- Default progression cadence: is 1h/4h/24h pattern acceptable as org default, or should we tune per-product?
- Who has rights to execute global kill switches? Product managers or only SREs for compliance reasons?
- Should we enable automated promotion based on signals or require manual sign-off for >10% promotions?
- Canary resource isolation: when to require dedicated capacity (Dedicated customers) vs in-path canary?

Small decision proposals (quick votes):
- Proposal A: default to signal-based promotion for internal product launches; manual gating for customer-facing or enterprise-impacting changes.
- Proposal B: require that any rollout touching model variants with quantization changes run as shadow canary for 24h before in-path slice.
- Proposal C: restrict global kill switch execution to SRE on-call in first 6 months of adoption, after that expand to product on-call with training.

Appendix: quick checklist for templating in console UI:
1) Fill title, owner, jira
2) Attach dashboard link and baseline snapshot (24h prior)
3) Specify initial slice (percent and attributes)
4) Upload step-by-step progression with guard thresholds
5) Provide sample QA prompts and evaluator link
6) Confirm fallback variant and rollback steps
7) Run smoke test in staging and attach logs

Notes to self / rough ideas: 
- Could add a small lightweight CLI to auto-generate the rollout template from a PR description (reduce human error).
- Consider a ‘soft-stabilize’ mode where new variant is allowed slightly higher latency but is limited by token cost to avoid runaway pricing effects.
- Build a small library of pre-filled templates: internal-launch, enterprise-safety, model-quantization, infra-only.

References and links:
- confluence:RDW-2342-canary-guidelines (detailed definitions)
- jira:INF-1123 (recent incident with cache exhaustion)
- github:repo/rollout-configs (example YAML configs)

If you’re reading this and own a rollout soon: ping me (Maya) and Diego and we’ll run a quick pre-flight 15m check. This doc is deliberately light — will iterate into a formal playbook once we run a few more launches with the continuity-first primitives.

End of notes.
